Pollinators face steep declines, threatening the sustainability of crop pollination services. Seminatural habitat restoration and wildflower plantings can help mitigate pollinator declines and are subsidized by agricultural conservation programs; yet, management tools to identify where to prioritize pollinator conservation actions are lacking. Evaluating the response of plant species to climate change and predicting changes in their potential distributions are crucial for developing effective species conservation and management strategies. Oreorchis patens, a widely distributed orchid species in the northern temperate zone, is an important component of the temperate orchid flora due to its strong cold resistance, unique summer dormancy characteristics and strong asexual reproduction ability. In this study, six species distribution models were constructed based on the Biomod2 package. By comparing the parameters, the optimized MaxEnt model was finally used to predict the potential suitable habitat of O. patens within a five-country study areas in East Asia, which will be of great significance for the biodiversity conservation of this orchid species. item.title: Migration strategy and colonization: the disproportionate role of partial migration
item.description:
相关度 72.0 · 提出部分迁徙者更易定殖新区域，可解释分布与预测全球变化下的定殖物种

Colonization drives diversification and determines how species shift their ranges, making it central to ecology and evolution. As both seasonal migration and dispersal depend on locomotor capacity, migration could be a major yet overlooked route to colonization. Here, we present evidence that partially migratory species are disproportionately successful in founding new populations, whereas strict migrants establish more rarely despite routinely reaching potentially suitable habitat in novel areas. Building on the threshold model of migration, we propose that partial migrants’ liability to migrate lies closer to the threshold and/or is more environmentally sensitive, allowing displaced individuals to settle. This mechanism can help explain species distributions and diversification and predict which species might colonize newly suitable areas under global environmental change.

Tropical‐origin invasive plants are increasingly expanding towards higher latitudes. Two well‐recognized strategies can facilitate this process: evolving enhanced cold tolerance or phenological adjustment that enables reproduction within a shortened growing season. However, whether plants can coordinate these strategies to facilitate poleward range expansion remains largely unknown. We reconstructed the 109‐year invasion history of Ageratum conyzoides (Asteraceae) in China using historical distribution records. To assess cold adaptation, we quantified cold tolerance and its physiological and biochemical basis through common‐garden experiments across six populations spanning the species' latitudinal invasion gradient. Urbanization poses various threats to bird populations worldwide, of which bird‐window collisions (BWCs) contribute to a significant proportion of human‐related bird mortalities. Due to regional biases in collision research and a lack of model systems for identifying multi‐scale drivers and vulnerable species, little is known about the impact of collisions on European bird populations and the effects of various ecological factors on collision rates at larger scales. Here, we used long‐term ringing‐encounter data from Finland's national bird monitoring scheme to identify the vulnerability of Finnish bird species to BWCs and predict spatiotemporal dynamics of BWCs across the country. We observed BWCs in almost half of all breeding bird species in Finland, with species‐specific collision risks being significantly associated with habitat preferences. The Asiatic cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus venaticus), once widespread, now survives only in Iran, with its population nearing extinction. In this study, we synthesised 13 years (2012 to 2024) of monitoring data to assess demographic and spatial patterns of this critically endangered subspecies in Iran. Using extensive camera trap surveys across eight reserves, supplemented by published records of cheetah occurrences on social media, we identified 24 adult cheetahs in the Northern and Southern Landscapes. No reproduction or new individuals have been recorded in the Southern Landscape for over a decade, while the Northern Landscape supports the remaining population, likely fewer than 30 adult individuals. The species–area relation (SAR) has been extensively studied over the past century, yet the sources of variation around an estimated SAR curve remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the sampling variance of the SAR can be decomposed into two additive components: 1) conditional variance, assuming that regional richness is fixed and represents uncertainty associated with local sampling; and 2) an additional component attributable to uncertainty in regional species richness, including uncertainty arising from rare species that remain undetected in the regional sample. We establish this decomposition mathematically and evaluate its behavior through numerical simulations. Marine protected area (MPA) networks, as regionally connected local interventions, may address both local and regional threats, yet the impacts of MPA network design on adaptive processes remain unclear. The world is experiencing unprecedented rates of biodiversity loss. To reverse this trend, signatories to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) have committed to conserving at least 30% of marine and terrestrial areas by 2030, with an emphasis on sites critical for biodiversity. One mechanism to support this goal is the identification of Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) to inform spatial planning and the development of conservation area networks. However, few case studies demonstrate how the KBA process can be implemented in high-biodiversity, low-income countries. Nearshore marine habitats generate services worth billions of dollars, yet they are undergoing rapid, widespread degradation worldwide. Along northern California's coastline, a key habitat-forming annual species, bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana), has experienced historic declines of up to 95%. These losses have prompted efforts to uncover the mechanisms that influence kelp forest recovery, with the goal of restoring degraded habitats. Zoospore dispersal between neighboring populations is thought to be a key driver of recovery, yet the degree to which spore supply limits recolonization remains unresolved. A long-standing debate centers on whether persistent "gametophyte banks" fuel post-disturbance regrowth or whether recovery depends primarily on newly settled zoospores. Many of their impacts, including changes to water levels and vegetation, can be studied through remote sensing. Via a graphical user interface, users then generate a set of dam-absent locations for comparison and receive plots and numerical data indicating how indices associated with vegetation, water, temperature, and evapotranspiration change over time for dam-present and dam-absent locations.
